A list of three or more phrases,
written inline and separated by commas,
makes the reader count commas to find where each item ends.
Write it as a bullet list instead,
introduced by a sentence ending in a colon.
Use a numbered list when the items are steps done in order.

A run of parallel sentences is a list too,
even with only two items.
The common case is a set of resources,
such as videos or readings,
where each sentence names one resource and links to it.
Put each sentence in its own bullet,
so the reader sees how many resources there are
and where each one starts.

A series introduced by a colon is a list too,
even with only two items,
when the items hold math or links.
Write each item as a bullet,
and display any equation the reader must remember
(see @exm-colon-series).

A case analysis is a parallel run too.
Write one bullet per case,
and begin each with a bold label that names the case.

Say whether a list is exhaustive or exemplary.
Ezra Morrison's rule (2026-11-04):
"always specify whether a list is exhaustive
(with a lead-in like "X consists of the following categories:")
versus exemplary
(lead in with "for example: ", "including:", end with "etc", or similar)."
Without a marker, the reader cannot tell
whether an item left off the list is missing from the topic
or only from the list
(see @exm-exhaustive-exemplary).

Bullet lists matter most on slides,
where a reader scans a list rather than reading it as a sentence.
The rule is one case of a broader preference for more structure:
when content has a shape, show that shape in the markup.

A few mechanics to keep in mind when writing a bullet list:

- Keep the items grammatically parallel,
  so each one completes the introducing sentence the same way.
- Leave a blank line before the list;
  without it, Markdown reads the list as part of the paragraph above.
- Keep a short series of single words inline,
  such as "R, Julia, or Python".

::: {#exm-bullet-lists}

## Turning an inline list into bullet points

> ❌ Machine learning combines data to learn from, statistics to say what a finite sample of data supports, and optimization to find the model that fits the data best.
>
> ✅ Machine learning combines three components:
>
> - data to learn from;
> - statistics to say what a finite sample of data supports;
> - optimization to find the model that fits the data best.

The revised version puts each component on its own line,
so the reader sees at a glance that there are three.

:::

::: {#exm-resource-lists}

## Turning a run of resource sentences into bullet points

> ❌ Hastie and Tibshirani [extend least squares to several predictors](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o9hoLdylWKo). Starmer explains [multiple regression](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zITIFTsivN8).
>
> ✅ Videos:
>
> - Hastie and Tibshirani [extend least squares to several predictors](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o9hoLdylWKo).
> - Starmer explains [multiple regression](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zITIFTsivN8).

For the video notes this example comes from, see the DATA 571 chapter on
[linear regression](https://morrison-lab.github.io/lds/chapters/linear-regression.html).
Each bullet holds one video,
so the reader can pick one without parsing the paragraph.

:::

::: {#exm-numbered-lists}

## Turning inline steps into a numbered list

> ❌ k-means starts with $k$ group centers, assigns each point to its nearest center, moves each center to the mean of its points, and repeats until the assignments stop changing.
>
> ✅ k-means starts with $k$ group centers
> and repeats two steps until the assignments stop changing:
>
> 1. assign each point to its nearest center;
> 2. move each center to the mean of its points.

The numbers show the order of the steps,
and the loop condition moves into the introducing sentence.

:::

::: {#exm-case-bullets}

## Turning a paragraph of cases into bullet points

> ❌ At $z = 0$ the slope is $\dexpitf{0} = 1/4$.
> At $z = 2$ it is $\dexpitf{2} \approx 0.105$.
> At $z = -2$ it is $\dexpitf{-2} \approx 0.105$.
>
> ✅ The slope $\dexpitf{z}$ at three values of $z$:
>
> - **$z = 0$:** $\dexpitf{0} = 1/4$.
> - **$z = 2$:** $\dexpitf{2} \approx 0.105$.
> - **$z = -2$:** $\dexpitf{-2} \approx 0.105$.

The labels let the reader find a case at a glance,
and the bullets show that there are three.

:::

::: {#exm-colon-series}

## Turning a colon series with math into bullet points

> ❌ Derive the other two formulations: minimizing the negative log-likelihood $\argmin_{\vcoef}\ \sb{-\llik(\vcoef)}$, and empirical risk minimization $\argmin_{\vcoef}\empriskf{\vcoef}$ with $\emprisk = \tfrac1\nobs\sum_i \lossf{\outvar_i, \prob_i}$.
>
> ✅ Derive the other two formulations:
>
> - minimizing the negative log-likelihood, $\argmin_{\vcoef}\ \sb{-\llik(\vcoef)}$;
> - empirical risk minimization, $\argmin_{\vcoef}\empriskf{\vcoef}$, with
>   $$\emprisk = \tfrac1\nobs\sum_i \lossf{\outvar_i, \prob_i}.$$

Each bullet holds one formulation,
and the definition of the empirical risk is displayed rather than buried in the sentence.

:::

::: {#exm-exhaustive-exemplary}

## Marking a list as exhaustive or exemplary

> ❌ The metrics computed from a confusion matrix are:
>
> - accuracy;
> - sensitivity;
> - specificity.
>
> ✅ A confusion matrix for a binary classifier consists of the following four cells:
>
> - true positives;
> - false positives;
> - false negatives;
> - true negatives.
>
> ✅ Metrics computed from a confusion matrix include:
>
> - accuracy;
> - sensitivity;
> - specificity;
> - etc.

The first lead-in reads as exhaustive,
yet a confusion matrix yields more metrics than the three listed.
The second lead-in says the four cells are the whole set,
and the third says its list is a sample.

:::
